question: The wiretapping scandal has been plaguing the Greek political and social scene since 2020, with the surveillance of Greek politicians, military personnel, journalists, business people, judges, state officials and others through the National Intelligence Service system or the use of illegal Predator software1.

In fact, the surveillance by the National Intelligence Service was supposedly carried out for ‘national security reasons’, which have not been disclosed despite the decision of the Council of State that deemed the universal and total prohibition on informing the affected individuals of surveillance completed on them to be unconstitutional2.

However, beyond the critical questions that remain unanswered within the country, the surveillance of Greek ministers, senior military and other officials leaves open the possibility that their conversations with other European ministers, senior military and other officials were monitored, both in the context of bilateral contacts (e.g.

telephone communications or meetings) and in the context of their participation in meetings of EU institutions and bodies (e.g. EU ministerial meetings, meetings of the EU Military Committee). In view of the above: 1.

How will the Commission help to investigate whether European officials have been victims of surveillance due to their communications with Greek ministers, military or other officials who were monitored by the National Intelligence Service or via Predator?

Does the Commission intend to request information from the Greek authorities and contribute to the full clarification of the wiretapping scandal in Greece in order to investigate the above possibility?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.7.2026) The Commission takes allegations concerning the unlawful use of spyware and the surveillance of the communications of its staff very seriously. At present, the Commission has no information indicating that its staff were either specifically or incidentally targeted in the context of the reported surveillance of communications referred to by the Honourable Member.

Nor has the Commission been requested to assist in any related investigation. Should information emerge suggesting that Commission staff may have been affected, the competent Commission services would take all necessary steps to verify and investigate the matter.

More generally, following the 2023 recommendations made by the Committee of Inquiry to investigate the use of Pegasus and equivalent surveillance spyware (PEGA Committee)1, the Commission has further strengthened its security framework and enhanced cooperation with the other EU institutions under the coordination of the Computer Emergency Response Team for the EU institutions, bodies and agencies (CERT-EU).
